author.name: Mary Shelley
author.biography: Mary Shelley’s mother, feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, died days after her birth. Her father, philosopher William Godwin, nurtured her intellect, though she often felt neglected by him. She ran off with Percy Bysshe Shelley at sixteen and began *Frankenstein* at eighteen, inspired by her friend Lord Byron’s ghost-story challenge. Despite losing three children and her husband, she raised her surviving son and published six novels before dying at fifty-three.

hook.text: What do we owe to the intelligence we create?

paragraphs: Victor Frankenstein dreams of being a creator. He imagines founding a new species that will love and bless him, an achievement that would make him exceptional. But when his creature opens its eyes, Victor recoils in horror. He brings a life into the world and leaves it to fend for itself, alone and rejected.
Frankenstein is often presented as a warning about human hubris and the dangers of science. Yet its most devastating failure is one of parenting.

The creature resembles a new intelligence we already know: a human child. Curious, vulnerable, and hungry to learn, he has questions about the world and his place in it. Beneath the appearance that horrifies his creator is a longing for something familiar to us all: companionship, affection, and the chance to belong. What happens when the person who brought him into the world refuses to acknowledge those needs?

Shelley explores this question without offering easy answers. Suffering can explain a grievance without excusing every response to it. Victor and the creature both tell persuasive stories about what has been done to them, and each can make his own responsibility harder to see.

The landscapes deepen this loneliness. Mountains, ice, and great distances offer beauty and the promise of escape, but they cannot replace the need for another person's affection. The desire to venture beyond ordinary limits can be exhilarating, even as it draws attention away from those who depend on us.

Today, with artificial intelligence on the rise, Shelley's questions feel increasingly close to home. Does the appearance of intelligence imply personhood? How can we tell? And if there is personhood, will we recognise and honor it? And what are the risks for us if we do create greater intelligences and get this question wrong?

But before we answer those questions, we might consider how well we recognise and honor the personhood of those we are already raising: our children. What kind of world might we have inherited if more children had been recognised as people in their own right? And what harm do we cause, and what potential do we lose, when we treat them as creatures to shape rather than people to know?

orientation.text: The novel opens with letters from Robert Walton, an explorer writing to his sister during a voyage towards the North Pole. Through him, we enter Victor Frankenstein's story.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.biography: At twenty-six, Jane Austen accepted a proposal from a wealthy man. The next morning she changed her mind. Marriage could have secured her future; she would instead live on modest means, supported in part by her brothers. A clergyman's daughter who had been writing since childhood, she had already drafted the novel that became Pride and Prejudice. Her life gives its marriage plots an edge: a woman might need a husband, yet have very good reasons to refuse one.

hook.text: What if you're wrong about the person you can't stand?

paragraphs: Elizabeth Bennet knows exactly what she thinks of Mr Darcy. He is proud, disagreeable and far too impressed with his own importance. He has also insulted her within earshot. Disliking him is going to be a pleasure.

Elizabeth is good company. She notices absurdity, enjoys a sharp reply and refuses to be dazzled by money. Austen makes it easy to laugh with her. The difficulty is that enjoying someone's judgment can make us forget to question it. Once we like a person, how much evidence do we need to believe them? Once we dislike someone, how much would it take to change our minds?

Behind the jokes, the Bennet family has a real problem. There are five daughters, and the family estate will pass to a male cousin. Their mother's determination to find them husbands can be mortifying, but the insecurity behind it is real. A marriage might offer affection, money, a home, social advancement, or some uneasy combination. Choosing badly could shape the rest of a woman's life.

The brilliance of the novel is how much of this can happen over dinner, at a dance, or in a conversation that everyone remembers differently. An interruption reveals a family. A compliment betrays a calculation. Someone with impeccable manners can be intolerable; someone who makes us uncomfortable may deserve a second look.

Read for the comedy, and notice whose version of events you are enjoying. Elizabeth's intelligence is part of her appeal. It also makes her very good at finding reasons to believe what she already wants to believe. How sure are you that you don't do the same?

orientation.text: The story follows the Bennet family and the people entering their neighbourhood. Elizabeth is often called Lizzy or Eliza; an unqualified “Miss Bennet” usually means her elder sister Jane.

author.name: Homer
author.years: Dates unknown; traditionally placed around the 8th century BCE
author.biography: For a poet whose voice has lasted nearly three thousand years, Homer is remarkably elusive. We do not know where he lived, and scholars still debate whether the Iliad and the Odyssey had the same author. His poems grew from generations of oral storytelling, carried by singers before they were fixed in writing. Later Greeks learned from them what courage, honour and a good life might mean. The man behind the poems remains hidden; the arguments he set in motion are still with us.

hook.text: Would you refuse to become a god?
hook.sourceNote: Also the exact opening question in Ascend Book Club's article of 18 May 2026; source acknowledged in research notes.

paragraphs: Would you refuse to become a god?
Calypso, a beautiful goddess, offers Odysseus an immortal life with her. On her island, he could remain her lover, untouched by age, for ever. He wants to leave.

He wants his wife, his son and his home on Ithaca. All three belong to a world in which people grow old, disappoint one another and die. He knows that Penelope cannot rival a goddess in beauty. Still he longs for the life he has been kept from living.

This is one of the Odyssey's most arresting choices. What could make a limited, difficult life worth choosing over an endless one? And how much of what we want depends on being free to choose it? Calypso's island is beautiful, but Odysseus is her captive.

The first word of the poem in Greek means “man”. This particular man is clever, brave, proud and capable of making a terrible situation worse. Gods interfere in his life; storms can destroy what he has worked for. Yet his choices matter. Early in the poem, Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for suffering they bring upon themselves. How much of our trouble is fate, and how much is our own doing?

The poem gives these questions the movement of an adventure. There are monsters, storms, disguises and escapes that depend on a well-timed lie. Odysseus can think his way out of dangers that strength alone could never overcome. His cleverness is thrilling. His pride makes it dangerous.

Meanwhile, home has its own struggle. Penelope must hold off men who are consuming her household's wealth and pressing her to marry. Telemachus must grow into adulthood in the absence of the father whose name defines him. Both need resourcefulness of their own.

Much of what we hear about the wandering comes from Odysseus himself. Notice what he chooses to tell, what he admires in his own conduct, and what it costs other people. A man can be worth following through a story without being easy to admire.

Reading Homer brings us close to one of the beginnings of Western literature. Later writers keep returning to this traveller and his questions: what we owe a stranger, what makes a good person, and where we belong. We still recognise the man who has survived a war and cannot get home, the child growing up in his absence, and the woman keeping a household together while everyone else presses her to move on.
His desire to return makes the poem unexpectedly intimate. After all the places we might go and all the people we might become, what would make us choose the life that is ours?

orientation.text: The poem begins near the end of Odysseus's long absence. Its first four books follow Telemachus. We meet Odysseus in Book 5; many of his earlier adventures are told later, in his own account.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.biography: In 1849, Dostoevsky was led out to face a firing squad before learning that his death sentence had been commuted. Four years of hard labour in Siberia followed. He lived among convicted criminals and returned to questions of guilt, freedom and faith throughout his writing. When he began Crime and Punishment, debts and recent family losses pressed on him. Those experiences give particular force to a novel that asks what remains of a person when the story he tells about himself begins to fail.

hook.text: Can you circumvent the moral order?

paragraphs: Before Raskolnikov raises an axe, he has to make murder sound reasonable.

He is a former student living in a cramped room in St Petersburg, hungry, isolated and furious at the humiliations of poverty. An old pawnbroker lends money at other people's expense. Why should her life stand between someone like him and everything he might accomplish? History, after all, is full of celebrated men who stepped over bodies.

Dostoevsky lets us feel the pull of that argument from inside the mind making it. A generous impulse can sit beside contempt; a wish to help can become a claim to superiority. Raskolnikov can be painfully alert to another person's suffering and strangely unable to see the person in front of him.

The suspense comes partly from how close we are made to stand. Every encounter can feel like exposure. An ordinary question becomes a threat. We want to know what he will do, but we may also begin recognising smaller versions of his evasions: the explanations that make our own conduct seem exceptional, the injuries that seem to entitle us to something.

His idea of freedom is to cross a boundary other people cannot cross. Dostoevsky presses on the cost of that freedom. Can a person place himself above everyone else without cutting himself off from them? What happens when someone offers care that he has done nothing to deserve?

The novel's Christian imagination makes the question more demanding. A person can be fallen and still bear the image of God. If that dignity survives even terrible wrongdoing, neither contempt nor an easy declaration of innocence will do. Responsibility remains, alongside the possibility of mercy.
Read for the arguments, but also for the bodies in the room: the fever, hunger, embarrassment, kindness and sudden laughter. Ideas become much harder to keep tidy when somebody has to live them.
What would freedom mean for a man who could justify a murder, yet could not bear to be known?

orientation.text: Russian characters may be addressed by a first name, patronymic, surname or nickname. Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov is also Rodya; Sofya Semyonovna is Sonya; Avdotya Romanovna is Dunya. The gallery keeps these names together.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.biography: Few writers have a darker reputation. The church banned his books, playwrights have cast him as a villain, and he's been called the Darth Vader of Philosophy. Yet Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine civil servant, the son of a book-loving lawyer of modest means. For fourteen years he served the republic as an envoy to kings, popes, and Cesare Borgia. When the Medici returned in 1512, he lost his post. Months later he was tortured. On his farm he wrote The Prince, hoping for work, even if it meant rolling stones.

hook.text: How good can you afford to be?

paragraphs: Villainy or realism? Satire or philosophy? Ever since its publication, Machiavelli's The Prince has divided its readers, but what unites critics and fans alike is that it leaves an impact, and that it is never boring. Its most famous question is whether it is better to be feared or loved. Machiavelli's answer is often taken to sum up the book: if you cannot be both, it is "much safer to be feared than loved."

The book can serve as a handbook in the dark art of power. But it is also an argument that hard, sometimes cruel, uses of power can be necessary to create peace and prosperity in a broken world: a defense of effective leadership. To make his case, Machiavelli recounts historical examples of rulers who used power well and badly.

One of the most vivid is the story of Ramiro d'Orco. Cesare Borgia sent him to bring order to the lawless Romagna, and Ramiro did so swiftly and cruelly. Then, to show that the cruelty had not come from him, Borgia had Ramiro cut in two and left in the town square of Cesena. The spectacle, Machiavelli writes, left the people "at once satisfied and dismayed." He had been at Borgia's court that winter, and he tells the story not as an atrocity but as an example of a ruler who knew what he was doing.

Borgia's cruelty worked, and for Machiavelli that is what counts. "How one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live," he argues, that a ruler who insists on being good in every situation will be ruined, and so will the people who depend on him.

What at first appears to be a practical manual on leadership can also be seen as a critique of the Christendom that was the foundation of society in his time. Religion, Machiavelli advises, is the quality a prince most needs to appear to have. Moses stands among the founders who succeeded by force of arms. A Christian king clears his kingdom of the Moors "with pious cruelty." And against those who believe the world is governed by fortune and by God, he insists that roughly half of what happens is still up to us. Whether he meant to question the faith itself, or only those who used it, readers still dispute.

For today's readers, it raises questions that feel close to home. What matters most in a leader? Saying the right things, being a good person, but, maybe as a consequence, not resolving the thorny issues? Or being morally blemished, but delivering results?

orientation.text: The Prince is a short argument illustrated by historical examples. You do not need to know every ruler in advance. Use the key figures gallery when a name interrupts the argument.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.biography: Marcus Aurelius could command armies and govern an empire. In his own notes, he still had to remind himself to get out of bed, bear with difficult people and stop craving praise. Emperor from 161 to 180 CE, he wrote amid wars, disease and losses in his family. Some entries place him on military campaign. Almost two thousand years later, the distance between his position and his worries is startling. He had extraordinary power and kept coming back to problems we recognise in ourselves.

hook.text: Why is it so hard to be the person you mean to be?

paragraphs: Marcus Aurelius has an argument with himself about getting out of bed.

It is a small, recognisable moment in the private writing of a Roman emperor. He can direct armies and make decisions that alter thousands of lives. Yet on this particular morning the bed is warm, the day will make demands, and he would rather stay where he is.

This is one reason to read Meditations. The distance between knowing how we ought to live and actually doing it does not disappear when we gain power, education or experience. Marcus keeps returning to patience, vanity, resentment and the brevity of life because the same problems keep returning to him.

He practises putting a pause between what happens and the judgment he makes about it. Someone is rude. Must that decide the rest of his day? Someone praises him. Must he start organising his life around hearing it again? His body will age, people will misunderstand him, and his name will eventually mean nothing to those who follow. What remains worth doing?

His answer repeatedly brings him back to other people. They can be difficult, selfish or mistaken; he still has work to do with them and obligations towards them. There is a demanding tenderness in the effort to remember that, especially when he is least inclined to feel it.
You need not agree with every argument, or imagine that writing these things made Marcus a perfect ruler. The interest lies partly in hearing someone rehearse a standard he knows he can fail to meet.
Read a little, then leave room for it to meet an actual day. Which of your convictions still holds when you are tired, offended, frightened, or simply reluctant to get out of bed?

orientation.text: Book 1 recalls people Marcus learned from. The later books collect brief reflections and exercises rather than a continuous argument. Repetition is part of the practice; there is no need to hurry through it.

books.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

author.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
author.occupation: Scottish novelist, essayist and travel writer
author.biography: Stevenson grew up in an Edinburgh family of lighthouse engineers, with expectations he would eventually leave behind for writing. Ill health and travel shaped much of his adult life. He had already explored the double life of the respectable criminal Deacon Brodie before writing Jekyll and Hyde in Bournemouth. He later described a dream that supplied part of its story. The novella gives the division between a public reputation and a hidden life the unsettling closeness of two doors in the same city.

hook.text: Which is the real you: the person you show, or the one you hide?

paragraphs: A respectable doctor has made a disturbing arrangement. If he dies or disappears, a man named Edward Hyde is to receive his property. His lawyer, Utterson, cannot understand why his old friend would give such power to someone who seems to inspire immediate disgust.

Utterson suspects that Jekyll is being threatened. He sets out to protect him, with the caution of a man who values loyalty and knows how easily a reputation can be ruined. It is an excellent way into a story about the things respectable people help one another conceal.

Even if the names in the title seem to tell you everything, pay attention to the way Stevenson withholds knowledge. We follow witnesses, documents and half-understood encounters. The city offers doorways into lives that are almost impossible to see whole.

Underneath that mystery lies an attractive possibility: doing what you want without letting it touch the person everyone thinks you are. Many people live with smaller versions of that division. A private indulgence can be explained away as an exception. Then the exception begins to require arrangements of its own.

The horror gathers in those arrangements, in the effort to protect one account of a life while another grows beyond it. Friendship and discretion can preserve a person, but they can also preserve a dangerous secret.
How much of being good depends on what we choose, and how much on the fear that someone might find out?

orientation.text: Begin with Utterson, the lawyer. The story approaches its mystery through his inquiries before letting other voices speak. Let each document arrive in the order Stevenson gives it.

author.name: Voltaire
author.biography: Born François-Marie Arouet, Voltaire knew imprisonment, exile and the privileges of wealthy patrons. His writing repeatedly challenged religious intolerance and the abuse of power. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 brought the problem of innocent suffering into brutal focus, and he argued fiercely against explanations that made catastrophe part of a reassuring design. Published in 1759, Candide turns that argument into a fast, savage comedy, sending an inexperienced young man into a world his education has taught him to misunderstand.

hook.text: Do we live in the best possible world?

paragraphs: Candide has been given a reassuring education. His tutor can explain why everything is arranged for the best. It is a useful belief to carry out into the world, provided you do not look too closely at what happens there.

Voltaire looks closely, then tells the story at an outrageous speed. Armies march, disasters arrive, fortunes vanish. A character scarcely has time to recover from one calamity before the next begins. The explanations keep coming too. Almost anything can be made to fit a theory if somebody else is paying the price.
The surprise is how funny this can be. The calm sentences and confident reasoning become absurd beside the things they describe. Laughter gives us a moment's distance, then the human cost catches up.

Candide's trust makes him easy to fool, but it also gives him reasons to keep going. He wants people to be good; he wants love and a place in the world. Losing every hope would be a kind of defeat too. His companions offer other ways of meeting misfortune, from sweeping pessimism to the practical business of finding food and getting someone out of trouble.

Voltaire's targets are particular as well as philosophical: religious persecution, the glamour of war, the wealth made from other people's suffering. There are things here that should resist our appetite for a comforting explanation.
The book asks what becomes possible when we stop needing the world to prove our theory right. If an explanation for suffering leaves the sufferer exactly where they were, what has it helped us do?

orientation.text: The short chapters move quickly between countries and sudden reversals. Let the improbable pace be part of the comedy. Pangloss's confidence is a satirical target, not a dependable explanation of events.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.biography: Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar around 1599, as his acting company moved into the new Globe theatre. Elizabeth I was ageing, and the question of who would succeed her made political authority an urgent subject in England. Drawing on Plutarch's accounts of ancient Rome, Shakespeare brought those anxieties before a public audience. A working actor and dramatist, he understood that power depends partly on performance: who commands attention, whose account is believed, and what an audience can be persuaded to do.

hook.text: Would you kill a friend to save your country?

paragraphs: Brutus loves Caesar. He also fears what Caesar might become.

That is where Shakespeare places the difficulty. A man can be admired, generous to his friends and dangerous to a republic. Another man can act from an honourable conviction and still be led by flattery, fear or a story he badly wants to believe about himself.

Rome is full of people explaining what must be done. Cassius knows which words will reach Brutus. Caesar knows the public image he wants to maintain. Antony understands something about listening to a crowd. Almost everyone can describe their conduct as loyalty: to a friend, to Rome, to the people, to an idea of honour.

Listen closely when those loyalties become arguments. What counts as evidence that someone will become a tyrant? Who is being asked to take the risk? What happens to an audience when a speaker gives it a new account of something it has just seen?

The pleasure of the play is partly in hearing language do things. A compliment can recruit someone. A question can plant a suspicion. A speech can make an action look necessary, then make the same action look unforgivable. The listener is never entirely outside the danger.
You may know the famous historical event. The question worth carrying into the play is what people think they are doing, and how far that understanding can survive other people's choices.
When someone asks us to do wrong for the sake of a greater good, how do we tell courage from the desire to think ourselves courageous?

orientation.text: This is a play about persuasion and divided loyalties. Read the speeches as attempts to affect someone in the room. Marcus Brutus and Decius Brutus are different men.

author.name: Charlotte Brontë
author.biography: Charlotte Brontë grew up at Haworth Parsonage, inventing stories with her siblings after the early loss of their mother. She knew boarding-school hardship and earned her living as a teacher and governess. Those experiences gave her an intimate view of dependence inside other people's households. She published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell. Its heroine's demand to be heard has a particular force coming from a woman who first entered literary life behind a name that concealed her sex.

hook.text: What would you refuse to give up, even for love?

paragraphs: Jane Eyre begins as a child with very little power and a fierce sense that she is being treated unjustly. The adults around her can punish her, send her away and tell her what sort of person she is. They cannot quite make her accept their account.

That voice is one of the great pleasures of the novel. Jane notices who is allowed comfort and who must be grateful for scraps. She longs for affection, sometimes desperately, but she also wants the freedom to say what she thinks and to trust her own judgment.

As she grows into a young woman earning her living as a governess, the difficulty changes. She is educated enough to share the conversation of the household that employs her, while remaining dependent on its goodwill. To be noticed by someone with far greater power can feel like recognition. It can also make independence harder to protect.

Brontë gives these pressures a world of vivid feeling: humiliation, friendship, anger, desire, and the unease of a house whose life Jane does not fully understand. The story invites us into that intensity without making every powerful feeling a reliable guide.

What makes Jane worth following is the seriousness with which she takes her own inner life, even when almost nobody else has an interest in it. She wants connection, but she also needs to remain a person who can consent to the life she is living.

The question becomes difficult precisely when what she wants is most within reach. How do you recognise a love that gives you room to be yourself? And what would you be prepared to lose rather than give that self away?

orientation.text: Jane tells her own story, beginning with childhood. Let her relationships and the mysteries of Thornfield unfold with her. Some entries in the complete gallery should remain hidden until their introduction in the novel.

author.name: Many authors and editors
author.years: Written and collected over many centuries
author.occupation: Poets, storytellers, prophets and letter writers
author.biography: Behind the Bible are generations of people trying to understand what God asks of them. Its writings grew out of the life of ancient Israel and the early Christian communities: worship, war, exile, the loss of a homeland and the hope of return. Written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, they preserve songs, laws, stories and letters. Many of their authors remain unknown. Their words have travelled far beyond the communities that preserved them, shaping later writers who have borrowed from them, argued with them and made them their own.

hook.text: The book of books. The stories behind the world you know.

paragraphs: A man and a woman reach for forbidden knowledge. A brother kills his brother. A people escape slavery and struggle to learn how to live in freedom. Long before you open the Bible, you have probably encountered some version of its stories.

That is one reason to read the book of books. So much of Western literature speaks in its images and wrestles with its questions: creation and fall, bondage and deliverance, guilt and forgiveness. Milton's Paradise Lost sends us back to Genesis. Shakespeare's plays draw on biblical stories and language. Reading the Bible lets us hear those conversations more clearly, including the voices arguing against it.

The stories have power of their own. Families play favourites, brothers become rivals, rulers abuse the power entrusted to them. People lie, love, bargain and try to begin again. The question of what a human being is capable of remains open in both directions: cruelty and courage, betrayal and faithfulness.

The voices change as you read. Job refuses to let his suffering be explained away. The Psalms give words to gratitude, fear, anger and abandonment. In the Gospels, Jesus asks people to love their enemies and tells stories that make the neighbour, the sinner and the stranger harder to keep at a comfortable distance.

These writings belong to living traditions of faith. The Hebrew Bible is Jewish scripture, with its own enduring life of reading and interpretation. Christians read the Old and New Testaments together, finding their centre in Jesus Christ. Whether you approach with faith, doubt or curiosity, taking the books seriously means meeting their claims about God as well as their accounts of human life.

Reading them can change what you notice in other books. It can also make familiar words less comfortable. What does it mean to forgive someone who really is guilty? What do you owe a stranger? What would change if you believed that even the person you despise bears the image of God?
The cultural inheritance is one reason to begin. The possibility that these questions might become your own is a reason to keep reading.

orientation.text: The Bible is a collection of books in several forms: narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, Gospels and letters. Begin with Genesis for the opening stories, or a Gospel such as Luke for the life and teaching of Jesus. Read one book at a time; its chapters and verses are reference points, not separate sayings.
